subject: ent
title: Oral, oropharyngeal and hypopharyngeal cancers

steps.tx: **Oral cavity cancer** most often affects the anterior tongue, floor of mouth, buccal mucosa, palate, gingiva and lip, and is usually **squamous cell carcinoma** driven by tobacco, alcohol and betel or areca nut chewing with **submucous fibrosis**. Suspect cancer in any non healing ulcer beyond three weeks, red or white patch, lump with **induration**, loose tooth or referred ear pain. Tongue and floor cancers spread early to neck levels one to three, so measured depth of invasion now guides staging and elective neck treatment.
steps.say: Any mouth ulcer that refuses to heal beyond three weeks needs an urgent biopsy because cancer stays at the top of the list. Velvety red patches carry higher danger than white patches, so both deserve prompt referral and sampling. Betel and areca nut chewing stiffens the mouth through submucous fibrosis and strongly raises later cancer risk. Cancers of the tongue and floor of the mouth travel early to the upper neck glands, and measured depth decides whether the apparently normal neck still requires elective treatment.

steps.tx: The mouth photo shows a lateral tongue **ulcer** present beyond three weeks with a hard **indurated margin** and an adjacent red **erythroplakia patch**. This matches the assessment step where any non healing ulcer, red or white patch, or lump needs urgent biopsy. In the exam, link induration and erythroplakia with the highest malignant risk, and remember that tongue cancers spread early to levels one to three, so depth of invasion guides **elective neck treatment**.
steps.say: This closeup photo presents a tongue ulcer that has lasted beyond three weeks with a firm raised edge and a nearby red patch. The edge feels hard because cancer has infiltrated the tissue, and red patches carry the highest risk of malignancy. Such lesions require urgent biopsy rather than repeated antibiotics. Tongue cancers involve neck nodes early, so measured depth guides elective treatment of the neck.

steps.tx: **Oropharyngeal cancer** now splits into two diseases: **HPV positive** disease of the tonsil and tongue base in younger patients, often with cystic neck nodes and better prognosis marked by p16, versus tobacco and alcohol driven HPV negative disease with worse response. **Hypopharyngeal cancer**, usually of the **pyriform sinus**, presents latest with dysphagia, painful swallowing, referred ear pain, hoarseness, weight loss and nodes, and carries the worst prognosis. Heavy smoking and drinking also produce second primaries across the upper aerodigestive tract through field cancerisation.
steps.say: Cancers of the tonsil and tongue base fall into two very different diseases with different outlooks. Disease driven by human papillomavirus strikes younger patients, forms cystic neck lumps and responds better to treatment. Disease driven by tobacco and alcohol behaves more aggressively and carries a poorer prognosis. Cancer of the pyriform sinus hides silently, so swallowing difficulty and ear pain appear late, and the same smoking field often grows second cancers in the lung and food pipe.

steps.tx: **Assessment** maps the primary tumour with examination under anaesthesia, biopsy and **p16 testing**, the neck with ultrasound guided node sampling plus CT or MRI and PET for advanced disease or **unknown primary**, distant spread with chest imaging, and the host with nutrition, dental, speech and swallow review plus smoking and alcohol cessation and anaesthetic fitness. A squamous neck node without a visible primary triggers tonsillectomy and tongue base sampling, while EBV testing points toward the nasopharynx and p16 toward the oropharynx.
steps.say: Careful assessment maps the primary tumour, the neck, distant spread and the fitness of the patient before treatment starts. Surgeons examine the throat under anaesthesia, take a biopsy and request p16 staining to reveal virus driven disease. The neck needs ultrasound guided sampling with CT or MRI, while advanced cases also require PET scanning and chest imaging. When a cancerous neck node appears without any visible primary, surgeons remove a tonsil, sample the tongue base and use EBV and p16 tests to trace the hidden source.

steps.tx: **Treatment** is multidisciplinary by stage: early oral cancers undergo surgery with clear margins plus sentinel or elective **neck dissection**, with **free flap** reconstruction for tongue and floor defects. Advanced or oropharyngeal disease often receives chemoradiation that preserves organs, with surgery reserved for salvage. Hypopharyngeal disease frequently needs combined treatment with laryngectomy decisions that balance voice against cure. Dental clearance before radiation prevents bone necrosis, while speech, swallow and feeding planning plus smoking cessation improve survival.
steps.say: Early mouth cancers undergo surgery with safe margins, and surgeons also treat the neck electively or sample the sentinel node. Large tongue and floor defects require free flap reconstruction to restore speech and swallowing. Many throat cancers receive combined chemotherapy and radiation that preserves the voice box, while surgeons reserve operations for residual or returning disease. Dentists must clear bad teeth before radiation protects the jaw bone, and stopping smoking with feeding support improves survival as much as the chosen treatment.
